cards.back: Turmeric. Earthy and golden, it colours curries and is added in small amounts.
Cumin seeds. Warm and nutty, often fried first in hot oil.
Coriander. Seeds are citrusy and mild; the fresh leaves finish a dish.
Green cardamom. Sweet and floral, used in chai and desserts.
Black cardamom. Smoky and big, for rich savoury dishes.
Clove. Strong and numbing, used whole or ground.
Cinnamon (cassia) bark. Sweet and warm.
Black pepper. The sharp heat in many spice mixes.
Red chilli. Dried, for heat and colour.
Green chilli. Fresh heat.
Asafoetida. A pungent resin used in tiny pinches; mellows when cooked.
Fenugreek. Seeds are bitter-sweet; leaves are fresh greens.
Dried fenugreek leaves, crumbled over rich gravies.
Mustard. The seeds and oil of north and east Indian cooking.
Small black mustard seeds that pop in hot oil.
Fennel seeds. Sweet, often chewed after a meal.
Carom seeds. Sharp like thyme, used in breads and fried snacks.
Indian bay leaf. Cinnamon-like aroma in rice and curries.
Nutmeg. Used sparingly in sweets and garam masala.
Mace, the lacy covering of nutmeg.
Nigella seeds. Peppery little black seeds for breads and pickles.
Saffron. The costliest spice; a few threads colour and perfume biryani and sweets.
Dried unripe mango powder, for sourness.
Dried pomegranate seeds, tangy.
Tamarind. Sour pulp for chutneys, sambar and rasam.
Black salt. Sulphurous and savoury, key to chaat.
A tangy blend with amchur and black salt sprinkled on snacks and fruit.
A warming blend of ground spices, added near the end of cooking.
A South Indian blend of lentils, chillies and spices for sambar.
A Bengali five-seed mix: fenugreek, nigella, mustard, cumin and fennel.
Curry leaves. Fried in oil at the start for a nutty, citrusy scent.
Ginger. Fresh, sharp and warming.
Dried ginger powder. Hotter and earthier than fresh.
Garlic.
Mint. Cooling in chutneys and raita.
Fresh coriander leaves.
Poppy seeds, used to thicken and enrich gravies.
Star anise. Liquorice-like, in biryani and masala chai.
Long pepper. A hot, sweet relative of black pepper used in traditional medicine and spice mixes.
A sour dried fruit rind from the west coast, used in curries and drinks.
Tempering: spices sizzled in hot ghee or oil and poured over a dish at the end.
